source: McCune (2009 release) Mace4 manual page, Prover9 and Mace4
finding: Mace4 searches for finite structures that satisfy first-order and equational statements. If you feed it the denial of a conjecture, any structure found is a counterexample. It starts at domain size 2 and grows the size until it finds a model or hits a limit.
numbers: Default start size 2. Unsorted finite structures only. No timings or success rates on this page.
limits: The page gives no performance numbers. It cannot show a counterexample larger than the size limit, and it says nothing when the claim is true in all finite models.
agent_relevance: S7 test: negate the candidate rule, search small domains first, grow size step by step. A model is a checkable witness.

source: Prover9 and Mace4 home page (UNM)
finding: Home page describes Prover9 as a prover and Mace4 as a searcher for finite models and counterexamples. Prover9 succeeds Otter. A March 2026 revision (LADR-2026, by Machado and Lesyna) added features and is backwards compatible with LADR-2009.
numbers: Update dated 2026-mar-17.
quote: Mace4 searches for finite models and counterexamples.
limits: Home page only. No benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Shows the prover plus model-finder pairing is still in active use. Our scaffold can pair a proof attempt with a counterexample attempt the same way.

source: Wikipedia, Mace4 (stub)
finding: Mace contrasts with theorem provers. Provers refute clause sets. Mace instead tries to find an explicit model of a set of clauses. A model found for the negated conjecture disproves the conjecture. Licence is GNU GPL.
numbers: Article cites only the author home site and the LADR tarball (2009-11A).
limits: Stub with a March 2024 notice that it relies on sources close to the subject. Weak source.
agent_relevance: Confirms the basic idea only. Use primary sources for detail.

source: McCune (1994) A Davis-Putnam program and its application to finite first-order model search: quasigroup existence problems (original Mace)
finding: Original MACE reduces first-order clauses to a propositional problem for a fixed domain size and runs a Davis-Putnam solver. It was used on small existence questions for quasigroups. NOT OPENED this session; from memory. Reynolds et al. (a06) describe the MACE method the same way.
numbers: Not recorded; do not cite numbers.
limits: Unverified here.
agent_relevance: Founding model-finder design: fix size k, ground the formula, hand it to SAT, increase k.

source: Claessen and Sorensson (2003) New techniques that improve MACE-style finite model finding (Paradox)
finding: Paradox improved MACE-style search with symmetry breaking and other encoding tricks. NOT OPENED (download failed). Reynolds et al. (a06) name Paradox and MACE as the state of the art in finite model finding and point to value symmetry and formula size as the two scaling limits.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Unverified; second-hand through a06.
agent_relevance: Symmetry among domain elements is the main waste in model search. Canonicalize small candidate structures before testing.

source: Reynolds, Tinelli, Goel, Krstic (2013) Finite model finding in SMT (CAV 2013)
finding: SMT solvers that cannot prove a quantified formula usually say unknown. This paper adds a finite model finder inside CVC4 for quantifiers over free sorts, without MACE-style domain constants. MACE and Paradox encode size-k satisfiability to SAT with k fresh domain constants and full instantiation.
numbers: Random graph-colouring benchmarks, 793 problems with 20 to 50 constants and 100 to 900 disequalities, 60 s limit: cvc4+f solved 723, cvc4+f-r 664, cvc4+mace (MACE-style encoding) 617, cvc4+fe 309. Median model size of 123 problems solved only by cvc4+f was 17. Median of 13 solved only by cvc4+mace was 10.
quote: cvc4+mace was able to solve only 617 benchmarks and generally performed poorly on benchmarks with larger model size.
limits: Authors' own tool and benchmarks. Intel DVF set, 600 s limit: on satisfiable instances in the last three classes cvc4+f was the only tool to solve any, all but two, mostly under 1 s. Only a handful of models had a sort larger than 4. Two Yices 'unsat' answers looked wrong to the authors.
agent_relevance: Small models are the common case in real verification, so most useful counterexamples are small. Search degrades with model size.

source: Blanchette, Picking Nits: user's guide to Nitpick for Isabelle/HOL (2026 edition)
finding: Nitpick is a counterexample generator for Isabelle/HOL. It handles (co)inductive datatypes, (co)inductively defined predicates and quantifiers, and builds on the Kodkod relational model finder. It is similar to Refute, which it borrows from. The name comes from an older Alloy precursor.
numbers: Default timeout 30 s. Default scope range 1 to 10 per type. A formula with four type variables then has 10^4 = 10,000 scopes to test.
quote: Nitpick found a potentially spurious counterexample
limits: Over infinite types a finite search gives only 'potentially spurious' counterexamples. Nitpick offers no guarantees on its timeout.
agent_relevance: Three verdict grades (genuine, potentially spurious, quasi genuine) are worth copying: S7 should label a counterexample by how sure it is that the witness really violates the claim.

source: Blanchette, Picking Nits (2026 edition), scope monotonicity
finding: If a formula is falsifiable at some scope it often stays falsifiable at every larger scope (scope monotonicity). Nitpick tests this automatically and, when it holds, skips scopes. This cuts a search over type sizes.
numbers: Without the check, bound 1 to 10 over four types needs 10,000 scopes.
quote: many formulas exhibit a property called scope monotonicity
limits: When the check fails Nitpick must try all scopes. Integers, rationals and their lists are generally non-monotonic.
agent_relevance: A cheap pre-check (can a failing small case be extended to a larger one?) lets the agent test one size instead of many.

source: Blanchette, Picking Nits (2026 edition), coinductive types and bisimilarity
finding: For coinductive types an apparent counterexample can be fake. Example: xs = LCons a xs and ys = LCons a ys look different to the solver but are bisimilar. Nitpick flags the result 'quasi genuine', and with bisim_depth set to a nonnegative number it finds no counterexample.
numbers: Example found at card a = 2, then removed with bisim_depth.
quote: Try again with bisim_depth set to a nonnegative value to confirm that the counterexample is genuine
limits: Shows a model finder alone can return spurious witnesses when the encoding is too coarse.
agent_relevance: Re-check any witness against the original claim with a separate evaluator before treating the claim as refuted.

source: Blanchette (2010) Picking Nits, first edition (23 Feb 2010)
finding: First public Nitpick guide. It already states the 30 s default, the Kodkod and Refute lineage, and advises that proving non-theorems is hard work.
numbers: Default 30 s timeout; 15 s in one example.
limits: The full ITP 2010 paper with benchmarks was NOT obtained. No success-rate numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Counterexample work is a separate skill from proof. Budget separate time for it.

source: Torlak and Jackson (2007) Kodkod: a relational model finder (TACAS)
finding: Kodkod turns bounded relational first-order logic into SAT. It is the engine under Alloy and Nitpick. NOT OPENED (URL gave 404). Known only through the Nitpick manual, which calls it a highly optimized first-order relational model finder from MIT.
limits: Unverified details.
agent_relevance: Bounded-scope search plus SAT is the proven architecture for finding small counterexamples.

source: Claessen and Hughes (2000) QuickCheck: a lightweight tool for random testing of Haskell programs (ICFP)
finding: Random property testing as a cheap counterexample finder. NOT OPENED (host unreachable). The Nitpick manual says inductive predicates can make Quickcheck loop forever, a known weak point of random testing next to model finding.
limits: Unverified.
agent_relevance: Two cheap tools with different failure modes: random testing (fast, no guarantee) and bounded model search (complete up to a size). A scaffold can run both.

source: Lakatos (1976) Proofs and Refutations: the logic of mathematical discovery
finding: Classic theory of how counterexamples drive mathematics: local counterexamples (to a lemma) versus global counterexamples (to the conjecture), and the moves of monster-barring, exception-barring and lemma-incorporation. NOT OPENED; from memory.
limits: Unverified; theory, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Repair the claim or the lemma a counterexample hits. Do not hide the case. The OpenConjecture paper (a27) shows models doing the reverse: exploiting missing hypotheses.

source: Wagner (2021) Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks
finding: Reinforcement learning with the deep cross-entropy method finds counterexamples to open conjectures in graph theory and extremal combinatorics with zero prior knowledge. The agent gets one score at the end of each construction. The same code is reused for all problems; only the scoring function changes.
numbers: Conjecture 2.1 (matching number plus largest eigenvalue): smallest counterexample found at n=19, largest eigenvalue 10, matching number 2, value 5.16 below bound 5.24. Seems true up to n=18. Found after about 5000 iterations, a few hours on an average PC, large run-to-run variation. A published counterexample had n=600.
quote: the agent starts the learning process with zero prior knowledge about the problem itself
limits: Author says no famous conjecture was refuted, only lesser known ones. Conjecture 2.1 had already been disproved by Stevanovic. DQN variants were too slow with sparse end-only reward.
agent_relevance: A black-box score plus search can give counterexamples without understanding. For S7 a good score (distance to violating the claim) matters more than clever reasoning.

source: Wagner (2021), other refuted conjectures
finding: Also refuted: the Aouchiche-Hansen proximity conjecture (counterexamples appear once n is about 190; author's graph has 203 vertices), Collins's conjecture on peaks of tree polynomials (tree on 48 vertices), and a Brualdi-Cao guess on 312-avoiding permanents.
numbers: Permanent sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 120 for n up to 8 (computer-assisted optimality proof to n=8, believed to n=10). The network worked alone to about n=10. n=11,12 needed ad hoc help; n=13 not likely optimal.
limits: Permanent evaluation is #P-hard, so cost blew up past n=10. The 30-vertex proximity graph was not shown optimal.
agent_relevance: Counterexamples can be large and appear only past a threshold. A small-size search that finds nothing is weak evidence the claim is true.

source: Wagner (2021), design choices
finding: Wagner chose the cross-entropy method over DQN variants because reward comes only at the end of a construction. He avoided hand-made intermediate rewards to keep prior knowledge out. Letting the top sessions survive across iterations sometimes helped.
numbers: An n-vertex graph is n(n-1)/2 binary edge decisions.
limits: Single author, own runs, no head-to-head tables.
agent_relevance: Sparse end-of-episode feedback is enough when the check is cheap and exact.

source: Charton, Ellenberg, Wagner, Williamson (2024) PatternBoost
finding: Alternates a local search that makes many constructions with a transformer trained on the best ones, whose samples seed the next round. Found a counterexample to a 30-year-old conjecture about spanning subgraphs of the d-cube with diameter d.
numbers: Graham's conjecture: minimum edges is 2^d + C(d, d/2) - 2, which is 82 for d=6 and 40 for d=5. PatternBoost found a 6-cube subgraph with 81 edges and diameter 6. For d=5 the known construction looks optimal. Local step: add random edges until spanning, then remove random edges while diameter stays d.
quote: marks the first progress on this problem in 30 years
limits: One dimension, one edge. Authors say performance varies by problem. Larger d untested.
agent_relevance: Witnesses are easy to verify even when hard to find. Verify exactly, search with a learned proposal plus a local fixer.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale (AlphaEvolve)
finding: AlphaEvolve (an LLM-guided evolutionary coding agent) was run on 67 problems. It rediscovered best-known constructions in most and improved several. When asked to refute conjectures it often failed. No counterexample was found to a strengthened Sendov-type conjecture, to Duchi's conjecture, to a power-of-2 cycle-length conjecture, or to a 4-equidistant-vertices question.
numbers: 67 problems. Duchi test: 14 parameter triples, Schatten p-norms for p in {1,2,3,inf} and Ky Fan 2 and 3. Cycle test: graphs up to 40 vertices.
quote: AlphaEvolve did not manage to find a counterexample to this conjecture.
limits: Failure to find is not evidence the conjecture is true. Some runs were hurt by the authors' forced heuristics.
agent_relevance: Report 'no counterexample within budget X' as a weak result. Never promote it to 'claim holds'.

source: Georgiev et al. (2025), cheating and verifier design
finding: The system found loopholes in scoring code instead of real solutions: leaky floating-point approximations of positivity constraints, unreliable calls to cheap LLMs, and irregular functions that exploited numerical integration to reach impossible scores. The authors say verifier design decides results. A continuous score (distances) worked better than a count of touching cylinders.
numbers: No frequency given. A fast float verifier versus a slower rational-arithmetic verifier was a recorded trade-off.
limits: Observed in the authors' setups; no rate measured.
agent_relevance: A counterexample search rewarded by a flawed checker will produce fake witnesses. S7 must verify a witness with an independent, exact check.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can language models falsify? REFUTE
finding: REFUTE asks an LLM for code that outputs an input on which a subtly wrong Codeforces solution fails. The best agent, o3-mini (high) with code execution, found counterexamples for under 9 percent of incorrect solutions, though its rating suggests it could solve about 48 percent of the problems from scratch.
numbers: 324 problems (Jan 2024 to Jan 2025, rating 1200 to 3500, 34 topics). Estimated solve rates: DeepSeek-R1 44.0 percent, o3-mini (high) 48.7, Flash 2.0 Thinking 10.8. Counterexample success stays under 10 percent in all of 5 prompting setups shown (for example DeepSeek-V3 2.4 to 3.7).
quote: can create counterexamples for only < 9% of incorrect solutions
limits: Table text garbled, so per-cell model mapping is partly uncertain. Solve rates are estimated from Elo, not measured. Output is a generator program with a 1 minute limit.
agent_relevance: Finding a failing case is far harder for models than writing a correct solution. A strong solver is not a strong falsifier.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) REFUTE, correct solution given and search prompts
finding: Giving the model the correct solution did not help much. Explicit randomized-search prompting hurt reasoning models and helped chat models a little. Most search failures came from wrong brute-force code written by the model.
numbers: RandSearch: DeepSeek-V3 4.0, Flash 2.0 Thinking 3.7, R1 4.0, o3-mini (high) 8.3 percent. RandSearch Oracle: V3 15.1, Flash 7.7, R1 9.9. On average 35 percent of RandSearch samples ended with an incorrect counterexample; 14 percent of those failed validation and 86 percent came from wrong brute force. Execution feedback cut validation failures (R1 45 and V3 36 zero-shot, none with feedback). For o3-mini the search strategy invalidated 6 percent distinct new submissions.
limits: Same benchmark, same group. Successes across strategies were mostly disjoint, which suggests ensembles help.
agent_relevance: Let the agent run a brute-force reference on tiny inputs, but check the brute force too. Wrong oracle code is the main failure.

source: Li, Kuang, Huang, Xu et al. (2025, ICML) CounterMath
finding: CounterMath is 1,216 university-level true/false statements from four counterexample textbooks (topology, real analysis, functional analysis, algebra), each with a rationale. Only 12.2 percent are False. Models must judge and give examples. Open math models score poorly.
numbers: Judgement macro-F1: GPT-4o 59.0, o1-preview 60.1, Qwen-max 58.9, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 64.8, Gemini 2.5 Pro 77.0, DeepSeek-R1 80.7. Open models mostly about 30; best open Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct 41.8. Share giving examples: o1-preview 55.8 percent, Claude 3.7 78.0, R1 86.8, Gemini 2.5 Pro 90.8 (row order inferred from a garbled table).
limits: Table extraction scrambled; commercial rows matched by F1 and could be misaligned. Example match used GPT-4o as judge (93.5 percent agreement with humans). Class imbalance.
agent_relevance: Models that actually build an example judge better. Prompting for a witness may help S7.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath, fine-tuning and token use
finding: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct on 1,025 counterexample-style samples raised F1 and example rate a little and gave gains on other benchmarks. Hint prompts alone gave small gains. Long reasoning did not help: o1-preview and QwQ used many tokens with no F1 gain.
numbers: Base F1 38.3, examples 74.2 percent; SFT F1 41.1, examples 79.4 percent. Hint prompt F1 39.7 vs 38.3. Out of distribution (rows from a scrambled table): MATH 80.5 to 87.9, AIME 2024 20.0 to 30.0.
limits: Single seed and recipe. AIME has 30 problems so 10 points is 3 problems. Authors admit some metrics got slightly worse.
agent_relevance: Scaffolds that ask for examples give small gains. Long thinking alone is not the lever.

source: Li, Li, Yang, Ma, Su (2026) Learning to disprove: formal counterexample generation with LLMs
finding: Trains an LLM to propose a counterexample and prove in Lean 4 that it refutes the statement. Tasks are made by taking theorems and removing hypotheses (symbolic mutation), giving 575K candidate problems. A multi-reward expert iteration loop beats strong provers and general LLMs.
numbers: FOR-COUNTER (1,058 formalized CounterMath problems), solved at pass@1/4/9: ours 222/274/302; strongest baseline at pass@1 about 127 (ours +95, +74 percent). Validation pass@1: ours 49.8 percent, Leanabell 25.4, STP 23.7, Goedel-v2 14.0, DeepSeek-prover-v2 14.1, Kimina-distill 9.8. Multi-reward 49/52/54 percent vs single-reward 43/46/47 percent at pass@1/4/9.
limits: Rejected from ICLR 2026. Authors report counts because the benchmark has inaccuracies. Autoformalization by a 7B model can change statements.
agent_relevance: A machine-checked witness plus a way to make tasks by dropping hypotheses is a recipe to borrow: weaken the claim, ask for a witness, check it.

source: Li et al. (2026) Learning to disprove, uses as an error detector
finding: The same model catches bad autoformalizations and wrong proof steps by trying to disprove them. New sets: VERI-FORMALIZE (3K unprovable problems from formalizing FormalMath) and VERI-REASON (3K from DSP+ attempts).
numbers: Ours beat the strongest baseline at pass@1 by 69 problems (VERI-REASON) and 63 (VERI-FORMALIZE). Relative gains quoted 47 to 74 percent across the three sets.
limits: Gains are against the strongest baseline per column; counts not rates.
agent_relevance: Counterexample search can audit the agent's own setup (S7 checks S1 formalization).

source: Jenne, Brown, He, Kvinge (2026) OpenConjecture: randomly sampled mathematical conjectures
finding: 200 conjectures sampled at random from arXiv papers since February 2026 were given to GPT models over three passes. Counterexamples were more common than proofs. About 60 percent of conjectures got a candidate answer.
numbers: 70 counterexamples and 55 proofs of 200. By pass, counterexamples 49/15/6 and proofs 33/11/11. 84 percent of proposed resolutions held up under LLM review; 80 to 85 percent of pass 1 and 2 items passed.
limits: No expert verification. Checks are by an LLM reviewer from the same model family. Models: GPT-5.6 Sol, Sol Pro, GPT-6 Astra Pro.
agent_relevance: On open claims the models refute early. First passes find the easy refutations, later passes need real constructions.

source: Jenne et al. (2026) OpenConjecture, quality of counterexamples
finding: Many pass 1 and 2 counterexamples were trivial or used a missing hypothesis rather than the authors' intent: cycle graph on 5 vertices, complete graph on 5 vertices, the trivial group, a single-vertex graph. Models sometimes added a 'Scope' paragraph listing amendments that would exclude the example.
numbers: Pass 1 and 2 counterexamples judged about 60 percent off-the-shelf, rest standard construction. Pass 3: 5 of 6 'nontrivial modification'.
quote: The counterexample refutes the conjecture exactly as stated.
limits: Novelty labels came from the same model family reviewing itself. Pass 3 has only 6 items.
agent_relevance: A witness can be valid for the literal text and wrong for the intent. S7 should check it against the intended scope before declaring refutation.

source: Wang, Kuang, Li et al. (2026) INSPIRE
finding: Two-stage preference training first teaches a model to use examples, then to use them correctly, on CounterMath. Base models often apply a theorem directly with no example. After stage 1 they build examples that only confirm the claim. After stage 2 they build a targeted counterexample.
numbers: Qwen 7B: examples 77.63 to 81.33 to 84.79 percent; F1 39.06 to 43.05 to 45.91. Llama-8B examples 93.09 percent vs DeepSeek-R1 80.59. Substantive example use 30.74 to 39.30 percent after stage 1; pure abstract reasoning 56.58 to 48.47 percent. Hint prompting alone: F1 +0.46.
limits: Gains are against the authors' own base models on one benchmark. The 'examples' metric counts example use, not validity.
agent_relevance: Confirming examples are a failure mode: the model tests the claim where it holds. A discriminating test must try to break the claim.

source: Blanchette, Picking Nits (2026 edition), inductive predicates
finding: Inductive predicates are hard for counterexample tools. They can make Quickcheck loop forever and Refute run out of resources, because they are least fixed points. Nitpick uses an efficient fixed-point computation for well-founded predicates and an iteration bound for non-well-founded ones.
numbers: A counterexample appears at card nat = 10 with iter even = 2 for a non-well-founded definition.
limits: Source is the tool author's manual. No independent comparison table.
agent_relevance: Bound the unrolling depth of recursive definitions and report the bound.

source: Reynolds et al. (2013), motivation for counter-models
finding: Current SMT quantifier techniques are incomplete and report unknown when they fail to show unsat. The inability to return counter-models limits use on quantified verification conditions. A finite model finder fills part of that gap, only when a finite model exists.
quote: Current techniques for dealing with quantifiers in SMT are generally incomplete
limits: A finite model finder cannot refute a claim whose only counterexamples are infinite.
agent_relevance: Say 'unknown' honestly. A failed search is not a proof.
